rationale: Evidence: iteration 4 (base_speed 1.1, kp 2.5, kd 0.3, narrow five-sensor array) is the best raced design at 302.3, up from 178.2 at base_speed 1.3. Oval finish rate rose to 55% (11 of 20), oval max_error fell to 0.054 (from 0.061), and oval line-loss events fell to 0.95 (from 1.25). Line loss is still present on every track (s-bend 1.25, slalom 1.15), and s-bend and slalom still end off track in all 40 trials. Iteration 2 showed that the 22.5 mm wide array does not fix line retention, so the narrow geometry stays. Iteration 3 showed that kp 2.2 with kd 0.25 scored lower, so the gains stay at kp 2.5, kd 0.3, ki 0. Oval mean finish time at 1.1 was 1.97 s, so there is time margin under 3.0 s for a further speed reduction. Change: lower base_speed from 1.1 to 0.9, a single-variable step that the Evaluator's stated rule supports (line_loss_events at or above 1 with max_error near 0.06). Each line-loss event costs about 15 points per unit of progress, so keeping the line is worth more than speed here. Expected result: line_loss_events fall toward 0.5 or less on the oval and s-bend, the s-bend and slalom gain progress, and oval completion stays near 50% or higher with completion_time still under 3.0 s. Hypotheses to test: (a) speed in bends, not sensor coverage, drives the remaining line loss, so lower speed should cut line_loss_events on the s-bend and slalom; (b) steering_oscillation on the oval (0.33 at kd 0.3) stays high, so if line loss is already low after this step, kd 0.25 is the next separate test. Measurements requested: per-track completion, progress, completion_time, line_loss_events, max_error and steering_oscillation, which show whether the speed drop helps line retention and whether time stays under 3 s.
